Original Owner, Sons Reunite With 1962 Pontiac Catalina 421 SD He Had New, They Last Saw It in 1972
13 photos
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage
Pontiac is no more, it died 45 years ago, when the division made its last V8, a 301-cuber, ending a streak of 14,620,000 eight-cylinders cast between 1955 and February 20, 1981. Sure, General Motors kept PMD of life support for another 29 years before pulling the plug for good in 2010. Which was 48 years after Pontiac released one of its most famous powerplants of all time, the incredible, amazing, fabulous 421 Super Duty. This father-sons trio held a special gathering to dad’s former race car he last saw in 1972.
Decades of American drag racing heritage condensed into a sunny afternoon when three members of the Sharp family gathered around a gleaming crimson 1962 Pontiac Catalina Super Duty. Captured by host Brian Gainey on the Real World Garage YouTube channel, the emotional reunion brought octogenarian racer Barney Lewis Sharp together with his sons, William and John, alongside the legendary factory lightweight race car affectionately nicknamed “Big Chief.”
For the trio, this gathering marked the first occasion in 54 years that all three men stood together beside the machine that shaped their family lore. John Sharp flew in from Oregon specifically for the event, having only seen photographs, magazine features, and video clips of the restored Pontiac for more than 50 years. Standing together, the family admired its remarkably authentic factory-fresh condition and finish.
The story of this remarkable automobile began in late 1962 at Lane-Moak Pontiac in Jackson, Mississippi, where dealership co-owner Colin Lane grew tired of an undefeated local 1957 Chevrolet Corvette 283-cubic-inch Fuelie. Determined to humble the sports car, Lane ordered the only 1962 Super Duty delivered in Mississippi and had it shipped directly to Nichels Engineering in Highland, Indiana, where specialists blueprinted the 421-cubic-inch V8 to legal drag racing specifications.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Built as 1 of only 88 factory lightweight Catalinas equipped with aluminum fenders, inner panels, hood, and bumpers that shaved 200 lbs off the curb weight, the 3,850-lb brawler also featured a rare factory cigar lighter requested by mechanic Lewis Sharp. Paired with a close-ratio Borg-Warner 4-speed manual transmission and a 4.30:1 rear axle, the Pontiac easily defeated the rival Corvette, which later won the national B/Stock drag racing championship.
Although the Lane-Moak Catalina had the speed to capture the national crown in Indianapolis, the dealership simply could not afford the travel expenses to enter the finals. Initially, Sharp wrenched on the car while his skeptical brother-in-law served as the designated driver. Ignoring warnings about its violent temperament, the brother-in-law pulled second gear during an early run, spun in a full circle, and slid onto an adjacent dirt oval track.
That terrifying lateral lurch occurred because soft factory rubber bushings in the rear control arms allowed the axle to shift under heavy torque, forcing Sharp to steer hard right whenever he grabbed second gear. His friend Billy “Peanut” Buck joked that spectators at the starting line could see the headlights as Sharp crossed the finish line sideways. After Lane-Moak retired the car in 1964, Sharp bought it for $850.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage With the Big Chief moniker painted on the flanks, Sharp campaigned the Pontiac for five seasons until 1969, recording a best elapsed time of 11.88 seconds at Biloxi, Mississippi, and a top speed of 122 mph at Monroe, Louisiana. At Monroe, a bitter rival constantly accused him of running an illegal displacement, so Sharp invited the critic to measure the bare cylinder bores for free before bolting the heads on.
After the rival inspected the factory block, Sharp reassembled the motor and launched wide open, holding the dash tachometer at 6,000 rpm to hit 120 mph through the traps. His stunned accuser admitted he would have demanded an immediate teardown had he not just seen the open engine himself. Throughout those years, Sharp usually took $10 in gas money instead of trophies, giving his hardware away to eager local children.
Rising racing costs forced Sharp to sell the Catalina in 1969, and 15 years later his son spotted it languishing outside a service station in Crystal Springs, Mississippi, for $1,000. Sharp declined to buy it back, opening the door for Ardmore, Oklahoma, restorer Eugene Riotte to acquire the rough hulk in 1987. When Riotte visited Sharp, the former racer generously gifted him the original 1962 dual-quad intake from his shed.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Sharp had removed that manifold years earlier to run a borrowed 1963 dual-quad setup that held the carburetors level, which a thief later stole from his house, taking parts worth $2,500 to $3,000 today. Because the original motor had been sold after 7 races for a dirt tracker, Riotte spent 24 years rebuilding the Catalina with a period-correct high-nickel 421-cubic-inch Super Duty block bored 0.045 inches over to 431 cubic inches.
Fitted with forged internals, 2.02-inch intake and 1.76-inch exhaust stainless steel valves, a 12.25:1 compression ratio, brass rear suspension bushings, and replicated factory chalk marks, the Pontiac debuted in July 2011 in Bowling Green, Kentucky. There, Sharp reunited with the car after 42 years as it scored 400 out of 400 points.
Purchased by Sam Wofford in 2019, the coupe was showcased on several YouTube channels, including automotive chronicler Lou Costabile’s (the second one attached below).
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage The fearsome reputation of the Big Chief stems from the broader legacy of the Pontiac Super Duty moniker, which spanned from 1960 to 1963 before returning in 1973 and 1974. Introduced in 1960 on the 389-cubic-inch V8 with a single four-barrel or Tri-Power induction producing up to 385 gross hp, the program expanded in late 1961 with the 6.9-liter 421-cubic-inch V8, installed in 155 Catalinas and 16 Grand Prix coupes for 1962.
While 7 additional 1962 Catalinas received the 389-cubic-inch engine, the dual-quad 421-cubic-inch Super Duty V8 was OFFICIALLY rated at 405 hp at 5,600 rpm and 425 lb-ft of torque at 4,400 rpm. Real output sat a lot closer to 465 gross hp at 7,000 rpm, with a torque of about 510 lb-ft.
In 1973 and 1974, Pontiac revived the badge on the 455-cubic-inch Firebird Formula and Trans Am, delivering 310 net hp in 1973 and 290 net hp in 1974.
Photo: YouTube/Real World Garage Early Super Duty cars offered a standard 3-speed manual, an optional Borg-Warner T-10 4-speed manual, or a Roto Hydra-Matic automatic, whereas the 1973 and 1974 models utilized a Muncie 4-speed manual or Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 automatic. Dominating both stock car ovals and drag strips, a showroom-stock 1962 Catalina 421-cubic-inch Super Duty sprinted from 0 to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds and ran the quarter-mile in 13.9 seconds at 107 mph.
In the dead of winter, in 20°F (negative 6°C), on a snow-powdered, unprepped surface, with two grown men aboard, and 150 lb of ballast in the trunk. That’s what Motor Trend scored back in January 1962 (they also calculated the 421 SD’s true output), and estimated that, on a good day, on a good strip, the big Catalina would’ve cleared the quick-quarter in mid 12s, at trap speeds above 115 mph, after the zero-to-hero sprint of 4.5 seconds.
Ordering that factory-engineered velocity back in 1962 demanded a serious financial commitment, as a base Pontiac Catalina coupe carried a sticker price of $2,725 before options. Selecting the complete 421-cubic-inch Super Duty engine and lightweight aluminum body package added more than $2,250 to the invoice, pushing the final price past $5,100.
It was a lot of money, but it bought a die-hard racer bragging rights over everything else on the road back then, from 413 Max Wedges and Chevy 409s to Ford 406s.
